entries.title: Sudan: US proposes expanding UN arms embargo
entries.summary: The US has called for a UN arms embargo for Darfur to be broadened to the whole of Sudan. The change would require Security Council approval, with Russia warning it would hurt the Sudanese army.
entries.content:
Africa

Sudan: US proposes expanding UN arms embargo

August 24, 2026

The US has called for a UN arms embargo for Darfur to be broadened to the whole of Sudan. The change would require Security Council approval, with Russia warning it would hurt the Sudanese army.

The United States on Monday proposed expanding an existing UN arms embargo for Darfur to cover all of Sudan.

The proposal was put forth by US Envoy Massad Boulos during a UN Security Council meeting in New York.

"The brutality of the war waged by the Rapid Support Forces [RSF] and the Sudanese Armed Forces has discredited their claims to be legitimate governors of the Sudanese people," said Boulos, who warned that "external financial and military support is fueling the conflict and risks drawing neighboring states deeper into war."

Boulos said the US wants to expand the embargo geographically as well as materially in order to cover unmanned aerial vehicles and related technologies. Moreover, the US plan would see the number of experts monitoring the embargo increased.

The Darfur embargo has been in place for two decades and will expire on September 12, 2026, if not amended or renewed.

An expansion would require a Security Council vote.

Sudan wants 'technical extension' but warns against hampering army

Sudan's UN envoy urged members to endorse a "technical extension" of the existing embargo while warning against changes that would hamper the army.

"Sudan suffers the most from weapons and their illegal flow. However, expanding such a sanctions regime will weaken the protection of civilians," said Al-Harith Idriss al-Harith Mohamed.

Russia, which holds veto powers in the Security Council, has voiced skepticism over changes to the existing deal, saying that expanding the embargo could impact the Sudanese army's effectiveness.

UN Sudan experts say sophisticated weaponry suggests 'external support'

Before Boulos articulated the US position, UN Under Secretary General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs Rosemary Di Carlo warned that a "worrying aspect of the conflict in Sudan is its increasing complexity."

"Sophisticated weaponry," she said, "continues to point to ongoing external support to both parties."

The UN's humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, also made note of the fact that, "in recent weeks, fighting in Sudan has been characterized by the heavy use of drones and localized ground combat in areas less affected by rainy season conditions."

The war in Sudan, now in its fourth year, has killed tens of thousands and displaced millions of civilians.

While Sudan's army holds sway in the country's central and eastern regions, western and parts of southern Darfur are under control of rival Rapid Support Forces.

Darfur, a vast western region the size of France, has seen some of the worst violence of the conflict, with repeated attacks on displacement camps and ethnic massacres that kill thousands at a time.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: US announces bid to further isolate Iran economically
entries.summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has outlined what he called "unprecedented" moves to isolate Iran economically. He said it will focus on third countries, warning those who don't comply will "share" in the isolation.
entries.content:
Iran

US announces bid to further isolate Iran economically

August 24, 2026

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has outlined what he called "unprecedented" moves to isolate Iran economically. He said it will focus on third countries, warning those who don't comply will "share" in the isolation.

The US on Monday announced what it said would be an "unprecedented" bid to constrict Iran's economy, by targeting its trading partners, as the  war in the Middle East continues with no real resolution or progress in sight. 

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's much-hyped press conference did not include any solid measures or announcements, but he said to expect them to follow fairly rapidly in the course of the week.

He laid out plans for what he called the "economic asphyxiation" of the regime in Tehran, implying this would be achieved in large part via secondary sanctions on Iran's trading partners.

"Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent told a press conference. "We are going to hold everyone accountable."

What did Bessent say about the plans?

Bessent called the program "Operation Economic Outcast" and again sought to liken it to the "Economic D-Day" mentioned last week by US President Donald Trump, an analogy that prompted ridicule because of how poorly it seemed to fit the circumstances.

"In the Second World War, D-Day marked the historic beginning of a campaign with our Allies to target and drive the enemy from its positions, including those in third counties," Bessent said, in an apparent effort to salvage the historical allusion.

It would target Iran "and its enablers," he said.

"Iran now faces a very clear choice, with only two paths before them: Complete global isolation and a subsistence economy, or a path back to normalcy with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy," Bessent said.

He said the Treasury had mapped "every node, every network, every facilitator that Iran has used to smuggle oil and evade sanctions," and said it would now start to "tighten the noose" to constrict "every potential source of revenue that funds the IRGC and the evil Iranian regime."

Carrot and stick both brandished at third countries

There would be a "zero leakage approach," he said, adding that for third parties it was "no longer acceptable to operate in the grey spaces of this conflict."

"The president is making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime. We are already seeing results," Bessent said, without elaborating.

"Those who stand with the United States will reap the rewards of our partnership," Bessent said. "Those who tether themselves to the Iranian regime should expect to share in the isolation of a withering regime."

He said the US would issue various countries a defined timeline to cooperate and steps to take, or to face consequences.

How has Iran responded to the new sanctions?

Responding to the latest US sanctions on Monday, Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh predicted "another defeat" for Washington, saying Tehran had a "two year plan" to counter the sanctions.

"They have done everything they could to test the determination of the Iranian people and the country's officials, but they have failed every time. It seems they wished to suffer yet another defeat," Madanizadeh told state television.

"We've been waiting for these plans for a long time, and the government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events."

Over the weekend, the head of Iran's top security body warned that Tehran would see any country's support of the US measures as an "act of war."

Supreme National Security Council leader Mohsen Rezaei said Iran would "retaliate in a seismic manner" to the sanctions by targeting other oil-shipping routes from the Persian Gulf.

"If the economic war ​continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf," Rezaei said.

Why is the US having to focus on third countries?

Iran has already been living under international sanctions for decades. The US does almost no bilateral trade with Iran and has very little direct economic leverage over it.

Prior to the war, Iran's two biggest trading partners by far were China — arguably the country and entity that has most effectively stood up to past attempts at economic intimidation from the Trump administration — and the United Arab Emirates. The UAE last week announced it was suspending all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran until further notice.

NATO member Turkey and neighboring Iraq both do a substantial amount of business with Iran.

Russia is also a valued trading partner, albeit one with no need of Iranian fuel exports.

Germany is Iran's largest European trading partner, but volumes barely exceeded a billion euros in 2025 (not much more than the US figures) with provisional government figures suggesting the levels will roughly halve to record lows this year amid the war.

Bessent said he would not "name names" when it came to whose cooperation the US would seek or demand.

Ahead of Monday's press conference, China's Foreign Ministry said Beijing was monitoring developments closely and would do what is necessary to protect its rights. The ministry also added that sanctions and pressure tactics do not help resolve problems.

'Economic D-Day'

In a post on X prior to Monday's announcement, Bessent described the sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary."

He said US President Donald Trump had "dismantled Iran's military capabilities," destroyed nearly 100% of its military factories and "buried its nuclear program."

"We are now entering the endgame," he added.

Hours ahead of the announcement on Monday, Trump said Iran was "completely collapsing" in a post on social media.

Last week, the US president announced what he called an "economic D-Day" for Tehran, threatening harsher sanctions targeting not only Iran but also countries that continue to do business with it.

"Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent said on Monday.

The current situation in the Iran war

The Middle East war began on February 28 when Israel and the US carried out strikes on Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Tehran responded with strikes on energy infrastructure and US bases in the Gulf region.

While the two sides have stopped the bombing, talks to end the conflict have stalled, with control over the Strait of Hormuz remaining a key sticking point. Iran has effectively closed the waterway, crucial for global oil and gas shipments, while the US maintains a blockade of Iranian ports.

Under a memorandum of understanding signed in June, the two sides had 60 days to negotiate an end to the war and reach an agreement on Iran's nuclear program. But that period expired last week with no signs of a deal.

Meanwhile, Pakistan's army chief was due in Iran on Monday as part of efforts to revive diplomatic talks in the conflict.

And on Tuesday, Oman's foreign minister is set to meet his Iranian counterpart to continue talks on the Strait of Hormuz.

Edited by: Rob Turner, Rana Taha

entries.title: DR Congo peace roadmap: Will the fighting finally end?
entries.summary: A new roadmap sets out the conditions toward peace in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). But disagreements over M23 rebels, Rwanda's role and security concerns remain, and could still derail the process.
entries.content:
Democratic Republic of Congo

DRC peace roadmap: Will the fighting finally end?

August 24, 2026

A new roadmap sets out the conditions toward peace in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). But disagreements over M23 rebels, Rwanda's role and security concerns remain, and could still derail the process.

Representatives of the Congolese government and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group agreed on a roadmap for peace after negotiations in Geneva.

It builds on the US-brokered framework signed in Doha last year, and sets out steps and timelines for negotiations and implementation: a ceasefire monitoring mechanism is also due to receive support from the UN peacekeeping mission, MONUSCO.

The United States, Qatar, the African Union (AU) and Switzerland have all expressed their support for the process as brokers of the push for peace.

However, it is not a full peace plan with bindíng resolutions and terms; rather, many aspects of the push will still need to be fine-tuned.

The new diplomatic initiative could nevertheless be offering fresh hope following years of bloody conflict in eastern DRC; fighting in the region has killed hundreds of civilians and displaced millions since 2022. The M23 rebel group continues to control large parts of North Kivu and South Kivu — two provinces in eastern DRC that are highly coveted for their minerals.

As disagreements remain over key issues, doubts continue to cast a shadow over the prospect of a lasting peace.

From signature to implementation

"There are likely to be many more bumps on the road — disagreements remain over issues including sanctions against M23, the release of detainees and the timing of political reforms. So this remains a very fragile commitment," Alex Vines, Africa program director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, told DW.

Conflict analyst Clifton Chifuwe, executive director of the Centre for Peace Research and Advocacy (CPRA), a local NGO that focuses on conflict management, agrees with that assessment, pointing to the presence of multiple armed groups in the area, the deep level of mistrust between DRC and Rwanda, and competition over eastern Congo's mineral wealth.

He believes that the biggest of the challenges across the board is to turn this roadmap into action.

"Signing it is easier than implementing it on the ground," Chifuweexplains.

Chifuwe told DW that independent monitoring mechanisms and the involvement of all key stakeholders will be essential for any peace to hold.

Rwanda's role in the conflict

Rwanda has repeatedly rejected accusations that it backs M23 rebels — though international groups maintain the view that the small neighboring nation is deeply entrechned in the conflict.

Kigali's relationship with the rebel group therefore remains central to the peace process, says Vines:

"Rwanda's good faith and its relationship with M23 is a really key consideration. Kigali's buy-in to any agreement and influence over M23 is key."

Rwandan President Paul Kagame's comments at a press conference on August 24 further underline the complexity of the issue; Kagame rejects the narrative that Rwanda is responsible for the current conflict, blaming factions within the DRC instead.

He links any Rwandan involvement in the conflict to what he describes as a longstanding security threat from the other side of the border, naming the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) armed group — which fights against M23 rebels alongside the Congolese military — as his main target.

Kagame said that "if this problem of the FDLR is not resolved," Rwanda would act to protect itself "at any cost."

Mixed messages of hope and skepticism

There also are signs and reasons for cautious optimism: Chifuwe highlights that the roadmap focuses on a sequenced implementation plan, with monitoring initiatives to be put in place to help identify warning signs before any violence resumes.

These international mediators will also have to maintain pressure on the parties while ensuring regional concerns are heard.

In this context, Vines believes that US and Qatari involvement remains important, while stressing that African input through the AU must not be ignored.

All parties involved have signed off on a pledge to "pursue negotiations towards comprehensive peace and conflict resolution" — for now.

What does peace mean for the displaced?

Ultimately, the roadmap will not be measured by the signatories' attitudes but by results for thousands upon thousands of people in the eastern DRC, who remain displaced.

"The real test is ... whether ordinary Congolese people become safer and better off," Chifuwe says emphatically, highlighting also the restoration of state authority and the management of mineral resources as key objectives that need to be achieved.

For Congolese civilians, the diplomatic language carries a personal meaning: One refugee named Linda Kasongo finds herself stuck in Zambia five years into the conflict.

She told DW that she wants to return home, but can't even entertain the thought, since violence on all sides continues to wreck lives and livelihoods in her war-torn home region.

"I hope it works out because I want to go home," Kasongo says. "I want to be with my people. I miss my people. I miss my home."

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: The new Bundesliga season is here, but has the glow gone?
entries.summary: Another Bundesliga season arrives, but are the golden years of Germany's top football league already over, and what can it do to change its course?
entries.content:
August 24, 2026

Another Bundesliga season arrives, but are the golden years of Germany's top football league already over, and what can it do to change its course?

The 64th season of the Bundesliga is here. The tiny team from Elversberg will become the 59th club to play in the league, Ismael Saibari is Harry Kane's new back-up at Bayern Munich, Schalke return after three years away, and Kathleen Krüger is Head of Sport at Hamburg. 

Coming off an XXL World Cup and a new broadcasting deal in the US, the Bundesliga is looking to step forward into a new era. But beyond the loyal support of club fans both domestic and abroad, has the international appeal of the league, particulary in the key US market, worn off?

"It would be hard to argue that the Bundesliga has not suffered some back-sliding in their standing. When Bayern and Dortmund met in the Champions League final [in 2013], I believed it was just the league announcing its superiority with intent to stay at the pinnacle of club football in Europe. I couldn't have imagined that might have been the brief apex," Randall, a US-based Cologne fan who has been watching the league for 16 years, told DW.

"Frankly, the Bundesliga has likely already seen its popularity at its peak. It is only downward from here."

Dominik Schreyer, a professor of sports economics at Germany's Otto Beisheim School of Management, doesn't believe that is the case though.

"I would be cautious about declaring the Bundesliga’s golden era over," Schreyer told DW.

"The league still has full stadiums, strong clubs, excellent players and coaches, and a distinctive football culture."

Schreyer does admit though, despite the league's great reputation of player and coach development, failing to retain players like Erling Haaland or Florian Wirtz makes it more difficult to increase the reach of the league.

"Bayern’s prolonged dominance has reduced uncertainty at the top, while the Premier League has developed a major financial and distribution advantage. The problem is therefore not simply a lack of talent or stories, but the Bundesliga’s limited success in turning those strengths into regular international viewing habits."

Club support strong, but league lacking luster

Robin Austermann, Bundesliga Americas executive vice president, said in the statement about the new Bundesliga broadcasting deal in the US that Bundesliga fans in America had grown by "43% over the past five years."

This is obviously a positive, although it would be intriguing to know how much growth had been made per year. For some fans though, beyond supporting their team, the league is lacking.

"Honestly, for pure viewing I prefer the Premier League since in their league at least three or four teams can win the title," Dave, a US-based Schalke fan since 1974, told DW.

"There is no doubt that both the Bundesliga and the second division are the envy of other countries from the attendance and management perspectives but I feel that the overall competitive sporting quality has declined. I absolutely believe that the Bundesliga has lost some of it's luster and reputation."

Cologne fan Randall agrees.

"You get a little drama around the border between the last Champions League slot and Europa League, but that doesn't really get the blood pumping how, does it? I still love watching the league, but I still have days on which I wonder if a Super League would really have been such a bad thing if it returned some competitive balance to the Bundesliga."

How can the Bundesliga change its course?

Much of the desire for change has to do with the lack of competition at the top. Bayern have won 13 of the last 14 titles. Some believe a more equitable distribution of TV revenue is a possible way forward.

"The market has become more fragmented, abundant, and competitive," Schreyer said.

"Availability no longer guarantees attention. Viewers increasingly encounter football through individual players, creators, highlights, short-form content, and major tournaments before deciding whether to watch full matches. The Bundesliga therefore needs a clear path from initial discovery to repeated viewing and, eventually, fandom."

Whatever the choice, the change needs to be made without losing what sets the league apart, namely the competitive ticket prices and passionate fan base. German football fans offered a vision for football in the country back in 2020 after the COVID-19 pandemic, but the gap between the rich and the poor in European football continues to widen.

"I think throwing out what makes German club football great in pursuit of competing in the market with the Premier League would be folly," Randall said.

Schreyer believes the major clubs and established stars are the strongest way to capture audiences' attention.

"Once viewers are engaged, the league’s wider strengths, including supporter culture, historic clubs, player development, Schalke’s return, and Elversberg’s rise, can deepen that interest," he said.

This Bundesliga season a pivotal moment for the league

Clearly, the US view is only one slice of the Bundesliga's market. Fan numbers doubled in Brazil between 2018 and 2024 to 24 million, and community initiatives through Bundesliga Common Ground have helped build interest in countries all over the world such as Thailand and Vietnam.

But the new deal in the US is perhaps revealing when it comes to the challenge the Bundesliga currently faces to position itself globally.

"A lot of fans were disappointed by the league’s move to go with Fandango this next season," said Jody, who has been watching German football since 2006.

"If the Bundesliga wants to grow in the US, they need to look at what NBC did when it won Premier League broadcast rights. It needs a more mainstream distribution in the US and more publicity of the league to draw new viewers in."

Schreyer argues that this is not the entire story.

"The new deal should ultimately be judged by whether it helps rebuild demand, not by potential reach alone," he said.

Criticism is something the Bundesliga has become familiar with in recent years. But off the back of a World Cup in the US, a key target country where a new broadcast deal was recently agreed, this feels like a pivotal moment for the league's development.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Trump says Canada to face 50% auto, steel tariffs from 2027
entries.summary: The latest threat comes after the neighbors failed to reach a deal to avert a 50% US levy on a range of other Canadian goods. Ottawa says it plans to impose retaliatory tariffs.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump says Canada to face 50% auto, steel tariffs from 2027

August 24, 2026

The latest threat comes after the neighbors failed to reach a deal to avert a 50% US levy on a range of other Canadian goods. Ottawa says it plans to impose retaliatory tariffs.

US President Donald Trump said Monday he would impose a 50% tariff on Canadian automobiles, car parts and steel from January 1, 2027.

The announcement comes amid an escalating dispute between the two neighbors following the collapse of trade talks last week.

"Build in the US ⁠and ​there are ​ZERO TARIFFS. ​Canada will be ‌treated like a ​[US] State ⁠no longer!" Trump wrote on social media, using his trademark all-caps style.

"On Trade, ‌and in other ways, also, ‌they ​are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and ​yet, WE DON'T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!" the US president added.

The current US tariff affecting Canadian autos stands at 25%.

Breakdown in negotiations

The two countries have blamed each other after failing to reach a trade deal late on Friday to avert US levies of 50% on a range of other Canadian products — from hockey sticks and fishing rods to wine and dairy products. Those tariffs went into force on Saturday.

The tariffs affect $20 billion (€17 billion) worth of goods, covering about 5% of what Canada ships to the US each year.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said his country would impose retaliatory tariffs from September 8 that would cover steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics.

The US currently accounts for roughly 70% of Canadian exports, making Ottawa potentially more vulnerable in the standoff.

No further negotiations are currently scheduled.

Trading blame

Carney accused Washington over the weekend of using "economic integration as a weapon" and said his country had been "attacked" by the new American tariffs.

"They asked too much and offered too little," Carney said.

US chief trade negotiator Jamieson Greer, meanwhile, said the US was compelled to act after a year of retaliation by its neighbor.

"We've said enough, and so we've taken countermeasures. Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains," he said.

Canada is yet to comment on the additional tariffs announced by Trump on Monday.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Iran protest victim: 'They were shooting to kill'
entries.summary: DW spoke with several Iranians affected by a brutal crackdown at the hands of the Tehran's security forces during the height of massive public protests in January.
entries.content:
August 24, 2026

DW spoke with several Iranians affected by a brutal crackdown at the hands of the Tehran's security forces during the height of massive public protests in January.

In January 2026, weeks before the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran, thousands of Iranians risked their lives in the largest and most widespread public uprising the regime in Tehran had ever faced.

The protests began in December 2025 amid grievances over economic hardship, but soon grew in scope and scale. 

The regime's security forces, made up of elements from the Ministry of Intelligence, the Basij militia, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), confronted the protesters on the streets with gunfire and beatings.

The scale of the crackdown drew international condemnation. At one point, US President Donald Trump threatened military strikes against the regime in response, telling protesters "help is on its way." 

But help never came. As the ensuing war overshadowed the aftermath of the bloody crackdown, support for the Iranian public in standing up against the regime fell off of the agenda.

There are no precise figures for the number of people killed or injured in the January 2026 protests. Iranian authorities have put the death toll at over 3,100.

However, Amnesty International stresses that because of the internet shutdown during the protests, the scale of the crackdown, and pressure on victims' families, the actual number of deaths is likely to be much higher.

The US-based Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRANA) confirmed over 7,000 deaths and investigated thousands more.

Fearing backlash, victims forego medical treatment

Seven months after the bloody crackdown, victims are dealing with permanent physical disability along with losing the opportunity to work or get an education.

Obtaining information from within Iran is both difficult and dangerous, and DW's interview partners chose to use pseudonyms for safety reasons. DW was able to contact victims through human rights networks.

One protester, Massoud, was buried just days ago, after months of enduring untreated wounds after being injured by hundreds of pellets during demonstrations in a city outside of Tehran.

According to relatives, who did not want to reveal their exact location, Massoud was first hit by pellets in the head. A plainclothes officer then shot him in the thigh and repeatedly kicked the wound, dislocating his femur from the hip joint.

Massoud struggled with his injuries for months. His relatives raised money for his treatment at home, and he underwent several surgeries, but the infection kept returning and spreading. Massoud in his final days declined further medical treatment, which his brother said had made him ashamed for being "such a burden" on his family.

Hamid Hemmatpour, a physician and board member of the Austrian Association of Health Professionals for Human Rights, told DW that fear of arrest and the insecurity of medical facilities forced many of the wounded to seek treatment at home.

Hemmatpour said the transfer and treatment of the injured during the protest crackdowns was catastrophic.

Some victims were transported in pickup trucks because of a shortage of ambulances, while others were suffocated en route to treatment while piled beneath the bodies of other wounded people.

"During two days of protests, around 2,000 injured people in need of hospitalization sought treatment at just one of the central hospitals in one of the cities, while the hospital had a capacity of 400 beds," he said.

"Security forces, meanwhile, were trying to take some of the wounded away while they were still in that condition," he added.

Iranian security forces 'shoot to kill'

Hemmatpour, citing reports from doctors inside Iran, estimates the number of injured at several thousand.

He told DW the most common injuries were to the head, neck and chest, followed by the abdomen and limbs. He added that most injuries were caused by live ammunition and automatic weapons. Targeting the head and chest, he said, may indicate shooting with the intention to kill.

Hemmatpour said that in some cases, security forces attacked people with knives and machetes in areas including southern Tehran after their ammunition ran out.

But much of what we know about the crackdown on protesters comes from human rights organizations.

The international non-profit organization Iran House documented victims like Naghmeh, a teenage student who lost an eye, or Mina, a pianist who lost the use of her fingers, and Milad, a runner who has lost a leg.

But consequences of the crackdown were not limited to protesters.

Mahshid Nazemi, a human rights activist and director of public relations at Iran House, said that some of those injured had not been taking part in the protests at all. These were people shot while shopping, returning from a party or standing outside their businesses.

Nazemi said that even families who filed complaints over indiscriminate shootings targeting their relatives were themselves subjected to prosecution by security forces.

Mahla, a 32-year-old woman and the sole provider for three children, worked in Tehran's bazaar before the protests. On January 9, while trying to get her teenage son out of a gathering, she was shot by Basij forces and hit by dozens of pellets.

Fearing security forces, she was treated at home for some time, but infections from her wounds eventually forced her to seek help from nurses she knew.

Seven months later, injuries to her right leg and wrist still prevent her from returning to work. Lack of insurance, financial pressure and a sudden increase in rent have also forced her to leave her home.

"They were shooting to kill. I wish they had killed me rather than leaving me disabled," she told DW.

I thought the regime was 'finished'

Nazemi said that some teenagers, after being injured, no longer want to continue their education. Psychological pressure on mothers, financial difficulties and family tensions have also increased.

According to her, some of those injured, from athletes and hairdressers to pianists and taxi drivers, have been forced to undergo amputations after severe injuries and infections, losing their jobs or their professional futures.

Ashkan was 17 when he was injured. Before the protests, he worked as a porter in Tehran's bazaar while learning jewelry-making, hoping to acquire a skill that would allow him to support himself and his mother.

He joined the protests in Tehran on January 8. He told DW that he thought Trump was going to attack and bring the Islamic Republic's rule to an end. Still, he left a copy of his will on the table as he left the house.

"I thought they would be finished by the evening, that we would go out and make some noise," he told DW.

"I was wearing a mask, and I was writing slogans on the wall of a mosque with some other young people from the bazaar when one of them fell to the ground," he said.

Ashkan said a bullet struck his friend directly in the heart; fired from a sniper rifle from a rooftop.

"When I raised my head, everything went black. I heard people saying, 'They shot him in the eye.' When I regained consciousness in the hospital, I saw that my left leg had been amputated below the knee. Everything was blurry."

Ashkan also lost an eye, and continues to suffer from serious complications.

"What has been taken from me is not just a leg and an eye; there is no longer any such thing as a future for me and my mother," he said.

Regime continues crackdown

The Islamic Republic's regime continues to pressure or kill those it considers linked to the January protests. 

In July and August 2026, 12 people were sentenced to death in connection with the so-called "Alikhani Square" case in the city of Isfahan. During the protests on January 8, authorities claim four government security forces were killed by demonstrators.

Five people have been executed so far in connection with the case, two of them publicly in the square.

And executions continue. According to a UN report, since March 19, 2026, at least 56 people have been executed on charges related to national security, 27 of them protesters from January 2026.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Myanmar: Why Rohingya refugees can't return
entries.summary: Nine years after the Rohingya were driven from Myanmar, claims of progress on refugee returns have revived talk of repatriation.
entries.content:
Myanmar

Myanmar: Why Rohingya refugees can't return

August 24, 2026

Nine years after the Rohingya were driven from Myanmar, claims of progress on refugee returns have revived talk of repatriation.

Myanmar's military-backed government is again talking about bringing Rohingya refugees home from refugee camps in neighboring Bangladesh. 

Earlier this month, authorities in Naypyidaw, Myanmar's capital, said they had made progress verifying Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh for possible repatriation.

Of the 820,000 names submitted by Bangladesh, Myanmar said it had verified around 308,000 as former residents but would not repatriate them until security conditions improve in civil war-torn Rakhine State.

But analysts told DW that large-scale, safe repatriation is now arguably further out of reach than at any point since 2017. Myanmar is engulfed in civil war, the military no longer controls most of Rakhine state, and the Rohingya are denied citizenship.

How Myanmar's Rohingya were driven from their homes

In August 2017, Myanmar's military launched sweeping operations in northern Rakhine state after alleged attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) militant group on security posts.

More than 750,000 Rohingya, a long-persecuted Muslim ethnic minority in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar, fled to Bangladesh, joining hundreds of thousands displaced by earlier crackdowns.

Muslim-majority Bangladesh now hosts around 1.2 million Rohingya refugees, mostly in camps around the southern coastal district of Cox's Bazar, according to UN bodies.

Myanmar does not recognize the Rohingya as one of its 135 officially recognized ethnic groups and has long referred to them as "Bengalis," implying they are migrants from Bangladesh despite generations of Rohingya having lived in Rakhine.

UN investigators found evidence of genocidal intent by Myanmar's military, while the United States argued in 2022 that members of the military had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya.

A genocide case brought by the West African nation of Gambia against Myanmar remains before the International Court of Justice in The Hague.

Myanmar's 2021 coup triggered a nationwide civil war that is still raging, even after a much-criticized election earlier this year saw the formation of a civilian government, which remains dominated by officials from the military and junta.

"Safe repatriation is simply not possible," Ronan Lee, a researcher at Loughborough University and author of the 2021 book "Myanmar's Rohingya Genocide," told DW.

There is a civil war in Myanmar and the economy has collapsed, Lee said, meaning a return under present conditions would carry a high risk of the Rohingya facing violence from the military.

"Myanmar's government is dominated by the same military that genocidally deported the Rohingya in 2017," Lee added. "Life in Myanmar today would be more dangerous for the Rohingya than when they were forcibly deported in 2017."

Safe return 'simply not possible'

Moe Thuzar, head of the Myanmar Studies Program at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, agreed that repatriation is much less realistic today than at any point since 2017.

Even if Myanmar's military-backed authorities wanted to facilitate returns, which few analysts think they do, they no longer control most of Rakhine, Thuzar noted.

The Rakhine-based ethnic Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group distinct from the Rohingya insurgent group ARSA, now controls much of the state, including northern areas from which many Rohingya fled.

UN reporting has documented serious abuses against Rohingya by both the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army, including restrictions on movement, arbitrary detention and forced recruitment.

Antje Missbach, professor of global and transnational migration and mobility at Bielefeld University in Germany, told DW that even if a voluntary return policy could be agreed, Myanmar's government has not offered the Rohingya citizenship.

Many Rohingya villages have also been destroyed, while others are now occupied by different communities, she added.

"Rakhine is not safe," she said, noting that hundreds of thousands of Rohingya are estimated to have left Myanmar for Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh over the past two years.

Camp crisis changes refugee behavior

Yet if returning to Myanmar looks increasingly unrealistic, remaining indefinitely in Bangladesh is also becoming more difficult. Funding shortages, mounting insecurity and a lack of opportunities to work or study are afflicting the camps.

"The worsening conditions in Bangladesh's Rohingya camps are fundamentally altering refugee behavior, pushing a population already traumatized by genocide into increasingly desperate and precarious survival strategies," Rafiqul Islam, a professor of peace and conflict studies at the University of Dhaka, told DW.

"The camps, which host nearly 1 million refugees, are facing a perfect storm of crisis: severe overcrowding, chronic underfunding, food ration cuts, limited educational and livelihood opportunities and growing security concerns," he added.

There has been an increase in Rohingya refugees trying to make dangerous sea voyages to Malaysia, Indonesia, or other Southeast Asian countries, while gang violence and other criminal activity are on the rise, Islam said.

There is also a growing trend of child marriage, child labor and school dropouts, "as families struggling with food insecurity are forced to make impossible choices between education and survival, sacrificing their children's futures for immediate needs," Islam added.

Food insecurity is now universal across the camps, according to the World Food Programme. UNICEF reported last year that admissions of Rohingya children for treatment of severe acute malnutrition had risen 27% year-on-year.

Mizanur Rahman, an anthropologist at Jagannath University in Dhaka, told DW that Bangladesh has legitimate concerns about bearing the burden of such a large displaced population, so the answer cannot simply be to ask Dhaka to do more. "There needs to be genuine international burden-sharing," Rahman said.

The UN and Bangladesh say $710 million (€608 million) is needed in 2026 for the most urgent refugee and host-community needs, of which around 60% has been funded.

The EU has allocated €23.4 million in humanitarian funding for Bangladesh this year, most of it supporting Rohingya refugees and host communities, and separately announced a €14 million development grant through UNHCR in June.

While the Rohingya remain unable to build permanent lives in Bangladesh, the conditions for a safe, voluntary and dignified return to Myanmar appear to have moved further out of reach.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Star violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter: 50 years on stage
entries.summary: Anne-Sophie Mutter constantly reinvents herself. For her 50th onstage anniversary, the star violinist is surprising audiences with sounds from around the world and never-before-recorded commissions.
entries.content:
Germany

Star violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter: 50 years on stage

August 24, 2026

Anne-Sophie Mutter constantly reinvents herself. For her 50th onstage anniversary, the star violinist is surprising audiences with sounds from around the world and never-before-recorded commissions.

The list of international composers who have written for star violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter is a long one. It features names like Krzysztof Penderecki and Sofia Gubaidulina, along with Andre Previn and Jörg Widmann. In recent years, women like Iranian-Dutch composer Aftab Darvishi and South Korean composer Unsuk Chin have also written works for Mutter.

On the occasion of the violinist's 50th stage anniversary, she's now recorded over 30 works either dedicated to her or commissioned by her — all part of her "ASM Forte Forward" project on the Alpha Classics label.

The first album in the series, "East Meets West," reflects not just the artist's musical passions but also her social engagement. The opening "Likoo for Solo Violin," composed by Aftab Darvishi for Mutter in 2024, leaves a powerful impression. "Likoo" is a lament about loss, written at a time when especially women in Iran were fighting repression by the regime.

Giving women a voice

"I wanted to create a musical tribute to the people in Iran and to those fighting for freedom, coexistence, empathy and equality, in the hope that these atrocities would never be repeated," Mutter told DW. "War is raging on our wonderful planet even as I'm playing, but I won't give up hope for love and empathy." Mutter's performance of it is deeply moving — one can almost hear the women's cries in the violin, fading into silence.

With the situation in Iran deteriorating, Mutter says it's especially important to her to keep "Likoo" in her repertoire. "I have great admiration for Persian culture and for the female composers who still live in Iran — such as Golfam Khayam, who managed to send me her score by email during a pause in the shelling. I still hear from her from time to time," Mutter says.

"These female composers in Iran fascinate me, and the piece 'Likoo' in particular. That's why — also sadly because of the current situation — it's very important to me to perform 'Likoo' at the anniversary concert." The concert is being held on August 25 at the Lucerne Festival.

Her 1976 stage debut in Lucerne

On August 23, 1976, a 13-year-old Anne-Sophie Mutter took the stage at a young artists' concert in Lucerne. It was there that conductor Herbert von Karajan first encountered the young talent. A year later, he hired her for a concert with the Berlin Philharmonic at the Salzburg Easter Festival. So began Mutter's long collaboration with Karajan and his Berlin orchestra.

Another figure who shaped her musical life on stage in the 1980s was Swiss conductor and patron Paul Sacher. "He was a major influence on my interest in contemporary music," Mutter says. She cherishes the undogmatic learning experience she gained from Sacher and her other mentors. Sacher always afforded her the freedom to decide how she would approach an assignment. He passed a motto on to her: "What I can't do, I can learn. What I can't learn today, I can learn later."

The Anne-Sophie Mutter Foundation

A four-time Grammy winner and recipient of Japan's Praemium Imperiale, she's now supporting highly gifted young musicians through the Anne-Sophie Mutter Foundation. She encourages her scholarship recipients to embrace social engagement alongside contemporary music. She's herself a supporter of humanitarian organizations such as Save the Children and Doctors Without Borders, and from 2021 to 2025 served as German Cancer Aid's chairwoman.

It's difficult for young musicians to build an audience and make money with contemporary music, Mutter says. "All the same, I want to keep them grounded and show them it's not just about getting rich and famous; they have a role to play in society — in social environments. Playing at a nursing home, for example, or teaching, supporting charitable organizations with benefit concerts."

A platform for composers

As well, Mutter uses the work she commissions — including from former and current scholarship recipients — to help advance their careers. "I want to give these pieces a platform, along with a recorded presence. Without that, these wonderful works couldn't be heard all over the world."

The next album in the "ASM Forte Forward" series being released for the anniversary is "American Tunes #1." It includes works by Andre Previn, whom Mutter was married to for four years, as well as US composer Sebastian Currier, who has written several pieces for Mutter.

"It gives me particular pleasure that many works by colleagues from my foundation, as well as by former and current scholarship recipients, have actually been recorded," Mutter says. "I have managed to put many of my young musicians at the center of this new 'Forte Forward' series, and that makes me very happy."

Albums of memories

To further mark her onstage milestone, Mutter has planned several projects with her longtime label, Deutsche Grammophon. Among them is the release of seven location-centered albums featuring selected works — pieces that, as in the case of the city of Lucerne, were premiered there or hold special significance in Mutter's musical life.

So far, "My Berlin," "My London" and, in connection with the anniversary concert in Lucerne, "My Lucerne" have been released digitally. The seven planned albums will follow the artist around the globe, from Berlin, London and Lucerne to Tokyo and New York.

Anne-Sophie Mutter's constant companion is her Stradivarius violin. "The violin is the coolest instrument in the universe. For 50 years I've tried again and again to show that," she says.

The instrument is her voice, too, she adds: "I find it fascinating how music becomes so expressive precisely where language ends, and how in this cosmos of creativity we can connect, discover ourselves, give ourselves over to expression, and truly experience life."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Syria sentences Assad-era top Muslim cleric to life in prison
entries.summary: Muslim cleric Ahmad Hassoun was convicted of crimes including inciting sectarian violence and justifying murder. He is the latest Syrian official aligned with ousted President Bashar Assad to face trial.
entries.content:
August 24, 2026

Muslim cleric Ahmad Hassoun was convicted of crimes including inciting sectarian violence and justifying murder. He is the latest Syrian official aligned with ousted President Bashar Assad to face trial.

A Syrian court on Monday handed a life sentence to Ahmad Hassoun, the country's former grand mufti under ex-President Bashar Assad.

The religious cleric, who vocally supported the regime's policies, was found guilty of a raft of crimes including inciting sectarian unrest and justifying murder.

Judge Fakhreddine al-Aryan said the official religious establishment under Assad had "justified the use of barrel bombs that targeted civilian areas and caused widespread destruction, which constitutes a violation of the rules of international humanitarian law."

A string of trials over civil war

Hassoun is the 10th Assad-era figure to be sentenced under Syria's new authorities.

Earlier this month, Assad himself and his brother Maher were sentenced to death in absentia for atrocities committed during Syria's civil war.

More than half a million people were killed and millions were displaced during the war, which began in 2011 following a crackdown on anti-government protesters. It ended in December 2024 with Assad's ouster in an offensive by Islamist-led militants.

The former president fled Syria as his regime fell and is believed to be in Russia.

Rights groups raise concerns

Death sentences have also been handed to Bashar's cousins, Atif Najib and Wassim al-Assad, who were tried in person.

The sentences have been welcomed by Syrians who had previously criticized the new government for not moving fast enough to act against Assad-era officials. But human rights groups have voiced concerns that the trials are being rushed and may not be fair.

"Advancing justice for the litany of serious crimes committed in Syria requires more than just convictions, but building a system that can deliver competent, impartial, and independent justice," said Balkees Jarrah, the Middle East and North Africa director for Human Rights Watch.

Who is Ahmad Hassoun?

Hassoun, 77, held the position of Syria's top Islamic cleric from 2005 until 2021, when the position was abolished.

An Aleppo native, he was known for his close ties to Assad and was often seen at his side on religious occasions.

He was arrested at Damascus Airport in March last year while trying to flee the country.

entries.title: Dutch pull out of 'no longer neutral' Eurovision
entries.summary: The Netherlands will not participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Bulgaria, the state broadcaster has said, citing divisions over the situation in Gaza. It's the second time the country is boycotting the event.
entries.content:
August 24, 2026

The Netherlands will not participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Bulgaria, the state broadcaster has said, citing divisions over the situation in Gaza. It's the second time the country is boycotting the event.

Dutch state broadcaster Avrotros said on Monday that the Netherlands will not be taking part in next year's Eurovision Song Contest (ESC).

The event can "no longer be considered neutral," given the war in Gaza, it said.

Eurovision boycotts

This year, the Netherlands was joined by Spain, Ireland, Iceland and Slovenia in staging the biggest political boycott in Eurovision history in protest at Israel's participation. Hundreds of pro-Palestinian protesters also marched outside the event. 

Avrotros Director-General Taco Zimmerman said international conflicts were increasingly affecting the contest and "undermining its neutral character," adding that it had "become a platform for division."

Earlier this month, ESC organizers announced new rules that bar any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.

"However, the recently announced ‌changes ... do not provide sufficient confidence that ​the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest ⁠has ​been restored," Avrotros ​said.

The pop spectacle is watched by tens of millions of viewers around the world each year.

Israel came close to winning the competition in 2025 and 2026, placing second in both events.

The 2027 ESC will be held in Burgas, Bulgaria, after singer Dara won this year's competition in Vienna, Austria.

The Netherlands and Eurovision: 'Very close to our hearts'

The Netherlands took part in the very first Eurovision Song Contest in 1956.

They have won it five times since then, most recently in 2019 with Duncan Laurence and his song "Arcade."

According to the Eurovision website, it was the first competition entry to reach 1 billion streams on Spotify.

The country's withdrawal from the next Eurovision is "painful as we would have very much liked to be part of the Contest again next year," Zimmerman said.

"As a public broadcaster, we remain committed to our values. They guide us in everything we do, even when that means stepping away from an event that is very close to our hearts," he added.

Edited by: Rob Turner
